name: Sittong
tagline: Darjeeling's orange village in the Riyang valley
meta_description: Sittong, the orange village near Kurseong: orchard season Nov–Jan, the Riyang river, the old church, homestays at ₹1,200–1,800 with meals and how to get there.
summary: Sittong is a village in the Riyang valley, about 25 km from Kurseong, in the heart of Darjeeling's orange-growing area. From November to January its orchards are heavy with mandarins. Homestays charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person with meals, and Latpanchar, Ahaldara and Namthing Pokhri are close by.

local_story.title: Oranges, cinchona and an old bamboo church
paras: Sittong sits in the valley of the Riyang river, which runs down from the ridges above Kurseong towards the Teesta. It is spread over three government land blocks, known locally as Sittong I, II and III, and its 3,098 residents (2011 census) live mostly by farming. The crop that made it famous is the Darjeeling mandarin, the small, loose-skinned orange grown on terraces and around houses all through the valley. When the fruit ripens from November, the village turns orange and green, and traders come up from Siliguri to buy.

The government cinchona plantations of the Mungpoo and Latpanchar area lie close by, and the Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December. Villagers will also show you their church. Local accounts say it began as a simple bamboo building more than a century ago and has since been rebuilt in brick; it still serves the Christian families of the valley, alongside the Hindu and Buddhist households around it.

did_you_know: Sittong had 3,098 residents at the 2011 census, with literacy of about 73 per cent.
The Directorate of Cinchona and Other Medicinal Plants, a West Bengal government body, has organised an orange festival at Sittong in December.
Sittong lies in the Riyang river valley, about 13 km from Mahananda Wildlife Sanctuary and about 20 km from Mungpoo.
intro: Sittong is a farming village, not a resort, and that is why people love it. The road winds down from the ridge through cardamom, broom grass, bamboo and terraces of oranges to scattered houses with flower pots on the verandas. In orange season the trees are everywhere, and families sell fruit by the kilogram from their doorways.

Come for a slow two or three nights. Walk down to the Riyang river and its bamboo footbridges, visit the old church, eat home-cooked food, and use Sittong as a base for Latpanchar's hornbills, the salamander lake at Namthing Pokhri and sunrise at Ahaldara. Homestays are simple and warm, and prices are among the lowest in the Darjeeling hills.
facts: Jio and Airtel patchy; better on the upper road
costs: Oranges in season, bought from the orchard

Local guide for a village and river walk

highlights.title: Orange orchards in season
highlights.text: From November to January, mandarins ripen on terraces all through Sittong. Walk among the trees, buy fruit from the families who grow it and watch the baskets being packed for the plains.

highlights.title: The Riyang river
highlights.text: A walk down to the Riyang river through fields and forest, with bamboo footbridges and clear pools. About 1–2 hours down and longer back up; good for a picnic in the dry months.

highlights.title: The old church
highlights.text: A small village church that, according to local accounts, started as a bamboo building more than a century ago and has been rebuilt in brick. Visit quietly and respect service times.

highlights.title: Base for Latpanchar and Ahaldara
highlights.text: Latpanchar's hornbill forests and the Ahaldara viewpoint are a short drive away. Do a dawn at Ahaldara and a morning's birding, then come back to Sittong for lunch.

highlights.title: Namthing Pokhri
highlights.text: The seasonal lake in the Shelpu hills where Himalayan salamanders breed in the monsoon is close by. A quiet half-day trip from Sittong.

how_to_reach.text: Most visitors hire a car. From Siliguri or NJP it costs about ₹3,000–3,800 and takes 2.5–3 hours, via Sevoke and the climb through Latpanchar, or via Kurseong. From Kurseong it is about 25 km via Bagora and Mahaldiram, 1–1.5 hours, ₹1,800–2,500.

A few local jeeps link Sittong with Kurseong and Siliguri, usually leaving the village early in the morning and returning in the afternoon. Ask your homestay for the day's timings; fares are about ₹150–250.
Many Sittong homestays arrange a car from NJP, Siliguri or Kurseong at a fixed price. Ask when you book and confirm the fare in advance.

where_to_stay: Sittong has many family homestays spread over Sittong I, II and III, typically ₹1,200–1,800 per person with dinner and breakfast. Choose by location: houses on the upper road have better access and phone signal, while those lower down are quieter and closer to the orchards and the river. Ask about attached bathrooms, hot water and blankets in winter. We do not name properties because they change often; recent traveller reviews and your Kurseong contacts are the best guide.
tips: Visit in December for the best of the orange season, and book early because rooms fill.
Buy oranges directly from orchard families; ask before picking anything.
Carry cash; there are no ATMs in the village.
Plan a car for the day if you want Latpanchar, Ahaldara and Namthing Pokhri together.
The walk back up from the Riyang river is steep; start by 9 am and carry water.

experiences.title: Walk the orange orchards of Sittong
experiences.summary: Walk the terraces of the Riyang valley in the orange season, from November to January, and buy mandarins from the families who grow them. Learn how the fruit is picked, sorted and packed for markets in the plains.
body: The Darjeeling mandarin is a small, loose-skinned orange, sweet with a sharp edge, grown for generations in the lower valleys of the hills. In Sittong the trees grow on terraces and around almost every house. From November the fruit colours, and by December the slopes are dotted orange.

Ask your homestay host to take you through the orchards of relatives or neighbours. You will see pickers on ladders, baskets lined with leaves, and fruit sorted on verandas into sizes for different buyers.
Buy a few kilograms directly. Prices are lower than in Siliguri and the money goes to the grower. Do not pick fruit yourself without permission; each tree belongs to someone.

faqs.q: When is orange season in Sittong?
faqs.a: Oranges ripen from about November, peak in December, and are mostly picked by late January. Exact timing depends on the year's weather and the height of the orchard. December is the safest month for a trip planned around the fruit.

faqs.q: Can I buy oranges from farmers in Sittong?
faqs.a: Yes. Most families sell fruit directly from their homes or orchards in season, usually for less than Siliguri market prices. Expect roughly ₹60–120 a kg depending on size and the year. Ask your homestay host who is selling.

faqs.q: Is Sittong worth visiting outside orange season?
faqs.a: Yes. March and April are pleasant, with spring flowers and good birding at nearby Latpanchar, and October is clear and green. The village is quiet and cheap all year. Avoid the heaviest monsoon months, July and August, when roads and paths are slippery.

experiences.title: Down to the Riyang river
experiences.summary: Walk down through terraces and forest to the Riyang river, with bamboo footbridges and clear pools. An easy descent and a steep return, best in the dry months.
body: The Riyang river cuts through the bottom of the Sittong valley on its way towards the Teesta. Village paths drop to it from the houses, past orange trees, cardamom under the shade trees, and patches of bamboo.

At the river, simple bamboo bridges cross between the banks. In the dry season the water is low and clear, with rocks to sit on and pools where village children swim. Have a packed lunch, then start back up by early afternoon: the climb is steep and takes longer than the walk down.
Go with someone from your homestay or a local guide. Avoid the river from June to September, when it rises quickly after rain and the paths become slippery.

faqs.q: How long is the walk to the Riyang river from Sittong?
faqs.a: Allow 1–1.5 hours down and 1.5–2 hours back up, depending on where your homestay is. The path is steep in places, with stone steps. Plan for 3–4 hours including a rest by the water.

faqs.q: Is it safe to swim in the Riyang river?
faqs.a: In the dry months some pools are calm and shallow, and village children swim there. Ask locals which spots are safe, never swim alone and stay out entirely in the monsoon, when the river can rise very fast after rain upstream.

faqs.q: Are the bamboo bridges safe to cross?
faqs.a: They are built and used by villagers every day, but they move underfoot. Cross one person at a time, hold the handrail if there is one and keep bags light. If a bridge looks damaged after rain, do not use it.

experiences.title: Sittong's old church and village lanes
experiences.best_time: Morning or late afternoon, any dry month
experiences.summary: Walk the lanes of Sittong to the village church, which according to local accounts began as a bamboo chapel more than a century ago and has since been rebuilt in brick. See how Christian, Hindu and Buddhist households share one valley.
body: Sittong's church is one of the village's landmarks. The local story is that the first building, more than a hundred years ago, was made of bamboo, like many early village chapels in these hills, and that it was later replaced with a brick building. We have not found a firm date, so treat the age as village history rather than record.

The walk there passes houses with flower-filled verandas, small shrines, prayer flags and kitchen gardens. Sittong, like most villages in these hills, mixes faiths easily, and festivals of each are shared.
Visit quietly, dress modestly, and avoid entering during services unless invited. Sundays are busy; weekday mornings are calm.

faqs.q: How old is the church in Sittong?
faqs.a: Local accounts say it started as a bamboo church more than a century ago and has since been rebuilt in brick. We have not found a documented founding year, so treat the age as village tradition. Ask the caretaker or your host for the story as they know it.

faqs.q: Can visitors enter the Sittong church?
faqs.a: Usually yes, outside service times, if the door is open. Dress modestly, keep your voice low and ask before taking photographs inside. On Sundays and church festivals, wait outside unless someone invites you in.

faqs.q: What religions are followed in Sittong?
faqs.a: Like most villages in the Darjeeling hills, Sittong has Hindu, Buddhist and Christian families, mostly Nepali-speaking. Festivals such as Dashain, Tihar, Losar and Christmas are all celebrated locally, often shared between neighbours.

experiences.title: Dawn trip from Sittong to Ahaldara
experiences.summary: Leave Sittong before dawn for the hilltop of Ahaldara above Latpanchar. Watch the sun rise over the Teesta valley and the Kalimpong hills, with Kanchenjunga to the north on clear mornings, and be back for breakfast.
body: Ahaldara is the open hilltop above Latpanchar, a short drive from Sittong. Cars stop below the top, and you walk the last few hundred metres up a path to the viewing area.

From the top the land drops away to the Teesta valley. On a clear morning you see the river below, the ridges of Kalimpong across it, the plains to the south and, if you are lucky, Kanchenjunga and its neighbours to the north catching the first light.

Book the car the night before through your homestay and confirm the fare. Dress warmly: the hilltop is windy and cold before sunrise from November to February. Stop at Latpanchar for tea and birds on the way back.

faqs.q: How far is Ahaldara from Sittong?
faqs.a: It is a short drive, roughly 30–45 minutes depending on where in Sittong you start, via Latpanchar. The last stretch to the top is a short walk of a few hundred metres. A car for the return trip costs about ₹1,200–1,800.

faqs.q: Can I see Kanchenjunga from Ahaldara?
faqs.a: On clear mornings, mostly from October to March, yes. The best chance is at sunrise before cloud rises from the Teesta valley. Even without the snow peaks, the view over the Teesta and the Kalimpong hills is wide and worth the early start.

faqs.q: What time should I leave Sittong for Ahaldara sunrise?
faqs.a: Leave about an hour before sunrise: around 4.30 am in April and May, around 5.30 am in December and January. Arrange the car the night before. Take a torch for the walk up and warm clothes.

faqs.q: Where is Sittong?
faqs.a: Sittong is a village in the Riyang river valley in the Kurseong block of Darjeeling district, West Bengal. It is about 25 km from Kurseong, 55–60 km from Siliguri, and close to Latpanchar, Ahaldara and Namthing Pokhri.

faqs.q: Why is Sittong called the orange village?
faqs.a: Because it lies in the heart of Darjeeling's orange-growing area. Mandarin trees grow on terraces and around houses all through the village, and from November to January the slopes are full of ripe fruit. A government directorate has organised an orange festival here in December.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Sittong?
faqs.a: November to January for oranges and clear views, with December the peak. March and April are good for spring flowers and birding at Latpanchar. Avoid July and August, when heavy rain makes roads and village paths slippery.

faqs.q: How do I reach Sittong from NJP?
faqs.a: Hire a car from NJP or Siliguri for about ₹3,000–3,800; the drive takes 2.5–3 hours. A few local jeeps run between Siliguri, Kurseong and Sittong, mostly early morning and afternoon. Many homestays arrange pick-ups at fixed fares if you ask when booking.

faqs.q: How much does a Sittong homestay cost?
faqs.a: Most charge about ₹1,200–1,800 per person per night with dinner and breakfast, as an indication for 2025–26. Prices rise slightly in December and on long weekends. Confirm hot water, bathrooms and blankets before booking.

faqs.q: How many days do I need in Sittong?
faqs.a: Two or three nights. One day for the orchards, the church and the village, one for the Riyang river walk, and a dawn trip to Ahaldara with birding at Latpanchar. Add Namthing Pokhri if you are there in the wet season.

faqs.q: Is Sittong good for families?
faqs.a: Yes. It is quiet, safe and cheap, and children enjoy the orchards and village life. The river walk is steep on the way back, so plan shorter walks for small children. Bring snacks and medicines, as shops are few.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network in Sittong?
faqs.a: Jio and Airtel work in parts of the village, better on the upper road than down in the valley. Do not rely on mobile data. Tell family your plans and download offline maps before you arrive.

faqs.q: Can I combine Sittong with Mirik or Darjeeling?
faqs.a: Yes. Sittong to Kurseong is about 1–1.5 hours and Darjeeling another 1.5 hours. Mirik is further, about 3 hours by car via Kurseong or Siliguri. A good loop is Siliguri, Sittong, Kurseong, Mirik and back to Siliguri in five or six nights.
